summary:
TERRAIN-X is a planetary-analog exploration prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It addresses the need to identify and characterize Earth locations that can serve as test environments for future Moon and Mars missions.

The platform brings Earth, lunar and Martian geospatial resources into a unified workflow, with interactive maps and 3D terrain views designed to support transparent comparisons of slope, relief and environmental context.

Its mission-based approach prioritizes evidence and data provenance rather than claiming that Earth sites replicate extraterrestrial conditions.

A complementary robotics module explores how a Unitree Go2 quadruped can acquire local LiDAR observations to add ground-level detail unavailable in orbital maps. The project also investigates immersive WebXR visualization.

TERRAIN-X aims to make analog-site screening more accessible, explainable and useful for planning robotic field tests.
details:
TERRAIN-X — Planetary Analog Discovery & Ground Truth

The Challenge

Selecting suitable terrestrial analog environments for lunar and Martian exploration requires analyzing terrain morphology, geology and environmental conditions. Although NASA provides valuable planetary and Earth observation datasets, combining these resources into an understandable workflow remains challenging.

TERRAIN-X explores how these datasets can help identify and characterize terrestrial environments suitable for testing future planetary exploration technologies.

Our Solution

TERRAIN-X is a modular platform organized into three complementary components:

1. Planetary and Earth Data Analysis

The scientific module is designed to combine NASA Earth observation resources with lunar and Martian cartographic data. It supports mission-specific comparisons using relevant characteristics such as elevation, slope, terrain morphology and environmental context.

The goal is to identify potential terrestrial analog sites and explain the supporting evidence, rather than treating visual similarity as proof of equivalent physical conditions.

2. Interactive Web Platform

The web platform provides an interface for exploring terrestrial and planetary information through maps and 3D visualization.

The interface design also explores WebXR and mixed-reality interaction, enabling more immersive inspection of terrain models and geospatial information on compatible devices.

3. Robotic Ground-Truth Exploration

A distinctive component involves the Unitree Go2 quadruped robot.

The robotics module explores how local LiDAR measurements and robot telemetry can complement orbital information by providing detailed observations of visible surfaces and obstacles.

This is an experimental terrestrial measurement approach, not a claim of direct robotic exploration of the Moon or Mars.

Innovation

The central idea is to connect planetary data analysis with physical observations.

Instead of offering only a visualization of planetary surfaces, TERRAIN-X proposes a workflow linking terrain comparison, supporting scientific evidence and local robotic measurements.

Technology and Development

The project uses a modular architecture separating geospatial analysis, the interactive web interface and robotic integration.

Development involves web technologies, Python-based integration and data processing, Git/GitHub, 3D visualization methods and experimental robotic connectivity.

AI-assisted development tools, including Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, supported programming, debugging, design exploration and technical documentation.

Expected Impact

TERRAIN-X could help research teams, engineers and educators explore and compare terrestrial test environments for future planetary missions.

Its long-term objective is to improve the accessibility, traceability and practical usefulness of planetary analog studies.

Limitations

TERRAIN-X is a hackathon prototype. Terrestrial analogs do not reproduce extraterrestrial gravity, atmosphere or radiation. Planetary visualizations, example data and robotic observations must be distinguished from scientifically validated measurements. Experimental features are documented according to their actual implementation status.
